title: Two ways to combine weak models
sub: Boosting adds models in sequence to fix what's left; bagging averages independent models to cancel noise.

frames.caption: Noisy data around a wavy trend. Boosting starts from the dumbest model: predict the average everywhere.
Round 1: compute the residuals, what the current model still gets wrong (orange, plotted around 0), and fit a one-split tree (a stump, green) to them.
Add 0.3 × that stump to the model. One step closer.
Round 2: compute the residuals, what the current model still gets wrong (orange, plotted around 0), and fit a one-split tree (a stump, green) to them.
Repeat: new residuals, new stump, add a fraction of it.
Each stump is weak on its own: one split. The sum starts to follow the trend.
Five rounds: a staircase approximating the curve.
Ten rounds. This is gradient descent in function space: each stump points down the gradient of the squared loss.
Twenty-five rounds: close to the underlying trend.
Sixty rounds: training error keeps falling...

...but by 200 rounds it is fitting the noise: training error is still falling while test error has crept back up (0.186 at 60 rounds, 0.199 now). That is why boosting uses a small learning rate plus early stopping.
Bagging takes the opposite route: one deep tree fits the data closely, noise and all (high variance).
A single depth-6 tree: jagged, chasing individual points. Test MSE 0.222.
Train 3 deep trees, each on a bootstrap sample (n points drawn with replacement). Each is jagged in a different way (gray).
Average them (blue): the jags partly cancel, because each tree's errors are different.

Average 50: much smoother, and test MSE drops from 0.222 to 0.195 with no extra bias. A random forest adds one more trick: each split considers a random subset of features, making the trees even less alike.
